s01.text: The handshake. Last time, your computer turned a name into a number. That solved one problem. It did not open a single connection.

s02.text: Right now, two machines know each other's address, and nothing else. Nothing is open. Nothing is agreed. One of them has to say hello.

s03.text: And you cannot just shout hello into the network. A packet can be lost, arrive twice, or arrive out of order. So before you send anything real, you agree on the rules.

s04.text: The client sends one packet. Syn. It carries a random number, its starting point for counting bytes. Not a password. Just a place to start counting.

s05.text: The server answers with two things at once. Syn, ack. Yes, I hear you, and here is my own starting number. And it repeats yours back, plus one.

s06.text: The client replies with a single acknowledgment. Three packets. One round trip. Now both sides have proved they can send, and that they can be heard.

s07.text: Three is the minimum. Two would leave one direction untested. The client would know the server can talk, but the server would never learn that the client's path works too.

s08.text: One round trip costs about thirty milliseconds. The budget is now seventy of two hundred. Thirty five percent, spent on saying hello.

s09.text: And still nothing is safe. Everything you are about to send is plain text, readable by every machine the packets cross. That is the next problem.

s10.text: Next, proving it is safe. Certificates, keys, and one more round trip.
